newsitem.title: USA: Albright says troops to have new Bosnia role.
newsitem.headline: Albright says troops to have new Bosnia role.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday that NATO-led troops in Bosnia would take on new roles to advance peace, including helping promote refugee returns and restoration of telecommunications links.

Albright announced the change during a U.S. Senate subcommittee appearance in which she said the United States had decided to rededicate itself to fully implementing the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords.

The shift is part of a new Clinton administration initiative to bring more incentives and pressures to bear to ensure that the rocky peace process -- in which it and NATO have invested so much -- is a success.

"Full implementation must be our goal in all sectors (of Bosnia) and the (Muslim, Croat and Serb) parties cannot pick and choose those elements they prefer at the expense of others," she told the panel.
"If they are not complying on key implementation tasks, it will not be business as usual for their politicians or their military leaders," she said.
Albright was expected to fully detail her plans in a speech in New York later on Thursday but her testimony to the Senate subcommittee on foreign operations gave an outline.

The NATO-led force would remain principally focused on enforcing the military aspect of Dayton. But she said: "It will build on its past accomplishments by actively supporting crucial civil implementation tasks within its mandate and capabilities.

"These include helping to create a secure environment for managed refugee returns and the installation of elected officials in targeted areas and specific economic reconstruction projects, which could include inter-entity telecommunications and restoring civil aviation," she said.
She was referring to telecommunications links among Serb, Bosnian and Croat communities.
The U.S. troops, the biggest component of the Bosnia peacekeeping force, are due to leave in June 1998.
Albright said it was important for "the international community, including both civilian and military components, (to) re-energise its commitment to implement Dayton."

The Pentagon has resisted calls for the Bosnian peacekeeping force to become involved in non-traditional activities, like tracking down indicted war criminals by the international tribunal at The Hague.

But other officials say the troops can and should be used for broader roles to secure the peace in Bosnia. Officials said the idea of creating a special unit to track down war criminals was still being discussed and remains a possibility.

She said the United States needs to be more assertive in supporting the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague. Earlier this week, the White House announced that a longtime aide of Albright was named special envoy on war crimes.

She began to get tougher with the Balkan principals this week when during a private meeting with Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic she scolded Zagreb for mistreating Serbs and other violations of the Dayton peace accords.
She warned then that Washington would oppose Croatia's bid for membership in NATO's partnership for peace programme and other western institutions unless Zagreb does better.
"Since Dayton was signed, our initial security goals have been achieved and economic reconstruction has begun," Albright told the Senate subcommittee.
"Unfortunately, there remain important areas where progress has been slow due to the failure of Bosnian leaders ... to embrace political and social integration," she said.
She reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to a single Bosnian state with two multi-ethnic entities -- the Moslem-Croat federation and the Bosnian Serb entity.
The new U.S. initiative would stress that only communities in Bosnia that allow displaced persons to return home would be eligible for international aid.

So far, four municipalities in Bosnia have been selected to participate in an "open cities" project and receive a total of $3.6 million in assistance. Another $5 million is still available to help repair buildings, provide agricultural support and business credit and to train workers in eligible communities.
Albright, who took a big interest in Bosnia when she was U.N. ambassador but had said little about it publicly since becoming secretary of state in January, plans to visit the Balkans next week.
In addition to Sarajevo, which had been announced, she will go to Brcko and Banja Luka, two of the most troubled symbols of the ethnic divisions.
